newsitem.title: USA: Albertson's skids on earnings projection.
newsitem.headline: Albertson's skids on earnings projection.

text.p: Shares of supermarket chain Albertson's Inc tumbled over 15 percent on Monday in a knee-jerk reaction to an announcement that earnings for its third and fourth quarters would be below analysts' estimates.
Albertson's topped the New York Stock Exchange loss-leader list, falling 6-5/8 to 36 in heavy afternoon trading.

The Boise, Idaho-based firm said it expects earnings per share for its third quarter to be about $0.42, well below the First Call consensus estimate of $0.48 a share. Albertson's said fourth quarter earnings should be about $0.61 a share.
Other retailers fell in sympathy. Kroger Co lost 2-1/4 to 42-5/8. American Stores Co lost 1-1/2 to 39-1/8 and Safeway Inc was 5/8 lower at 42.
"Valuations are real high out there and when people see (earnings disappointments) they sell now and ask questions later," said Gary Vineberg, analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co.
Vineberg is telling his clients to take some profits as valuations are too high.
"It has repercussions for the rest of the industry ... because other people are cutting prices and getting aggressive," he said.

Albertson's said it was facing increasingly stiff competition in some markets as other companies opened more stores. Vineberg believes that even those stores not expanding rapidly are vulnerable to the increased competition.

"There are a lot of stores being built in this industry, and the sales are not there to support a lot of the stores being built; and that tends to lead to price competition, and in the end if affects ... everybody," Vineberg said.
Joseph Ronning at Brown Brothers Harriman said that before this morning's sell-off Albertson's was trading high.
"Albertson's has been selling at a relatively high multiple for a supermarket," he said.
Nevertheless today's announcement came as a bolt out of the blue to Ronning and many other industry watchers.

"Albertson's is certainly the 'class' of the supermarket world and I think most people have just assumed ... good solid gains, and then all of a sudden this comes as a very rude wake-up call," Ronning said. "Even the best-run companies can have problems here and there."
Lesa Sroufe, analyst at Ragen MacKensie, was also surprised by the news but expects the problems will be quickly rectified. "I think they'll fix the situation in a couple of quarters," she said.
"The company has had very few surprises and the only surprises typically are on the up side, not the down side," Sroufe added.
Vineberg agrees that the problem will likely be a short-lived one, adding that the lower earnings were as much derived from management sticking to its guns as anything else.

"They had a choice of pulling back on some of these programs and trying to make the kind of earnings that people want, or running the business they want to run it and letting things run a more natural course," he said.
